title: The Chimney Sweeper (Experience): context
short: The companion to the Innocence poem, in Songs of Experience (1794): an adult questioner meets a child sweep, who answers with an accusation.
body: Blake drafted the poem in his Notebook, now in the British Library, before etching it for Songs of Experience (1794), where it answers the Innocence 'Chimney Sweeper'. The first two lines are the observer's, the third his question, and the rest is the child's reply. Where the Innocence sweeper accepts his lot and finds comfort in a dream of heaven, this child has seen through the comfort and blames his parents and the institutions they serve. Erdman's Prophet Against Empire places the Songs of Experience in the climate of the early 1790s: the French Revolution, Paine, and government repression at home.

title: 'A little black thing'
short: Blackened by soot against white snow, the child is seen first as a 'thing', not a person, which is how his society sees him.
body: The phrase reduces the boy to an object and a colour before he speaks. The black-and-white contrast which in Innocence separated soot from the white of the dream here sets the child against the snow. Blake's 'The Little Black Boy' in Innocence shows how readily he connected blackness with questions of human worth. The child becomes a person only when he answers, and the rest of the poem is his.

title: 'in the snow': the text
short: Blake's etched plate and his Notebook draft read 'among the snow'; the archive's 'in the snow' comes from a later printed text.
body: In Blake's own copies, and already in the Notebook draft, the line reads 'A little black thing among the snow'. 'Among' is slightly odd, as if the child were one more object amid the flakes, and it chimes with 'smil'd among the winter's snow' in l. 6. The text kept in this archive normalises it to 'in the snow'. Students quoting the poem should follow a standard edition such as Erdman's, or the plates themselves in the William Blake Archive.

title: 'weep! weep!'
short: The lisped street cry of the Innocence poem, but now the observer hears it plainly as weeping, 'notes of woe'.
body: In the Innocence poem 'weep' is the child's mispronounced 'sweep', and its double meaning is the reader's discovery. Here the observer names the lament at once. The phrase 'notes of woe' returns at the end of stanza 2, where the child says he was 'taught' to sing them. The sad cry is not natural to the child; it is a lesson imposed on him, part of the trade.

anchor: Where are thy father and mother?
title: The question
short: The adult's question exposes absent parents; in the Innocence poem the mother was dead and the father had sold the boy.
body: The observer's question, in quotation marks, sets up the dialogue, and the child's answer is the first shock: his parents are alive, respectable, and at church. Unlike the orphan of Innocence, this child has been put to the trade by living parents. In Erdman's text, following the plates, the line reads 'Where are thy father & mother? say?'; the archive's punctuation differs slightly.

anchor: gone up to the church to pray
title: 'gone up to the church'
short: The parents' piety is set against their neglect: religious observance becomes an alibi.
body: The rhyme 'Say'/'pray' is pointed, and 'gone up' suggests both the walk to church and a self-satisfied ascent. The parents can be at prayer while their child cries in the snow; churchgoing becomes a way of not seeing. The charge is developed in the last stanza and links this poem with 'Holy Thursday' and 'The Garden of Love' in Experience, where the Church is likewise a place of exclusion and restraint.

title: 'upon the heath'
short: The heath, open common ground, is the scene of the child's natural joy, the world of Innocence.
body: A heath is uncultivated open land, a place for play like the green of 'The Ecchoing Green'. The child's logic in stanza 2 is that his parents punished his happiness: because he was happy, they dressed him for death. Whether this is a real cause or a child's sense of injustice, it presents adult authority as hostile to joy. Blake's 'Proverbs of Hell' make the opposite case for joy, as in 'Joys impregnate. Sorrows bring forth.'

title: 'the clothes of death'
short: The sweep's black, sooty clothes are a shroud or mourning dress, and the trade itself kills.
body: Black was the colour of mourning, and the climbing-boy's clothes were black with soot. The phrase also recalls a shroud, as the 'coffins of black' did in Innocence: the parents have dressed the child for an early death. The rhyme 'heath'/'death' ties his lost freedom to his fate. The verb 'clothed' is pointed too: clothing children is a parent's first duty, and these parents have performed it in the deadliest way. The Innocence sweepers were 'naked and white' in their dream; this child is dressed for the grave.

anchor: taught me to sing the notes of woe
title: 'taught me to sing'
short: The sad cry is taught, not natural: his parents, and society, have trained the child into misery and its expression.
body: Repeating 'notes of woe' from l. 2 turns the observer's description into the child's own complaint, and 'taught' turns the trade cry into a lesson. His natural song was joy; his parents' teaching replaced it with woe. Glen and others see here Blake's interest in how social roles are learned and passed on. The line may also glance at the hymns that poor children were drilled to sing, as in the charity-school service of 'Holy Thursday'.

anchor: I am happy and dance and sing
title: 'dance and sing'
short: The child still has moments of play, which his parents take as proof he is unharmed; the sweeps' May Day dancing may be in view.
body: The child's resilience is used against him: because he can still be happy, his parents think 'they have done me no injury'. London sweeps were known for their May Day festivities, when they paraded with brushes and shovels, danced for money and accompanied the Jack-in-the-Green, as Joseph Strutt described in 1801. Spectators could take such dancing as evidence that the boys were content. Whether or not Blake has May Day in mind, the line exposes the comfortable reasoning of those who live off a child's labour.

title: 'no injury'
short: 'Injury' keeps its older sense of a wrong or injustice as well as bodily hurt; the parents believe themselves blameless.
body: From Latin injuria, a wrong (in-, 'not', and jus, 'right'), 'injury' in Blake's day still carried the legal sense of a violation of right, besides harm to the body. The child sees both. The weak rhyme 'injury'/'misery', resting on light final syllables, gives the stanza a falling cadence. The parents' complacency is the point. They have wronged the child in every sense, and their churchgoing assures them they have done nothing of the kind; the child's exact word convicts them.

anchor: God and his priest and king
title: 'God and his priest and king'
short: A satirical trinity of the Church's God, his clergy and the monarch, who together sanctify a society built on suffering.
body: The line yokes divine, clerical and royal authority, the alliance of Church and State that radical writers of the 1790s attacked. 'His priest and king' makes the God of conventional piety the patron of both. Blake is attacking not God as such but 'God' as the established Church presents him, an idea he develops in the 'Nobodaddy' verses of the Notebook and in Urizen. Erdman and E. P. Thompson relate such lines to Blake's radical and dissenting sympathies.

anchor: make up a heaven of our misery
title: 'make up a heaven of our misery'
short: The powerful compose, or fabricate, a heaven out of children's misery, profiting from it while preaching it as the road to bliss.
body: 'Make up' can mean compose, build or invent. The line implies that the heaven promised by Church and State is a fiction, and that the comfort of the powerful, their heaven here and now, is made of the poor's suffering. In the Notebook Blake first wrote 'Who wrap themselves up in our misery', then struck it out for the present line, moving from smug self-comfort to active construction. The line answers the Innocence dream: there the child was consoled by heaven; here he sees how it is made.

title: Form
short: Three quatrains: the first in couplets like the Innocence poem, the last two in alternate rhyme, as the child's voice takes over.
body: Stanza 1 rhymes aabb ('snow'/'woe', 'Say'/'pray'), like its Innocence counterpart; stanzas 2 and 3 switch to abab. The line is a loose four-beat measure. The change from couplet to cross-rhyme coincides with the child's taking over the poem, and his answer then runs for nine lines without interruption. The poem's twelve lines, against the Innocence poem's twenty-four, suit the compressed indictment typical of Experience.
